author.name: Plato
author.occupation: Athenian philosopher and founder of the Academy
author.biography: Plato belonged to the world of Athenian politics but made philosophy his life's work. He founded the Academy and wrote conversations in which strong claims are tested by other people. Socrates is their most persistent presence, asking questions that admiration alone cannot answer. Plato preserved a literary account of the trial of Socrates, his teacher. A city executing a man for the way he questioned it became a lasting problem for Plato's thinking about philosophy and public authority.

hook.text: Would you change your life to save it?

paragraphs: Socrates stands before an Athenian jury accused of corrupting the young and failing to honour the city's gods. His task, if survival were the only measure, would be to make himself reassuring.

The speech he gives makes another demand. He asks his hearers to consider whether being irritated by a questioner is a reason to silence him. He also explains why he cannot simply promise to stop doing the work that has brought him to trial.

Plato lets the courtroom become an argument about the price of an examined life. What do we owe our community, and what happens when the community demands that we abandon what we believe makes life worth living? Confidence can look like courage or provocation depending on where the listener stands.
Read as a juror as well as an admirer. When does someone else's refusal to make you comfortable become a service you are unwilling to recognise?

orientation.text: Apology means a defence speech, not an expression of regret. The work presents Socrates's defence and responses during his trial.
